abstract: This paper examines how monetary policy affects labor income inequality and whether these effects depend on overall economic conditions. Using monthly U.S. data, we show that standard linear models find little evidence of a relationship between monetary policy and inequality. Once we allow policy effects to vary with economic conditions, however, a clear pattern emerges. During normal periods, contractionary monetary policy temporarily reduces labor income inequality. During crises, the same policy shock produces a large and persistent increase in inequality. These opposing responses help explain why standard linear estimates find little overall effect. The joint state-dependent responses of labor market tightness and inequality are consistent with an important labor-market channel in the transmission of monetary policy. More broadly, the findings suggest that monetary tightening during periods of economic stress can carry particularly adverse consequences for labor income inequality.
title: Does Monetary Policy Affect Labor Income Inequality? Evidence from State-Dependent Transmission

abstract: This paper quantifies the effects of college expansion under purely merit-based, competitive admissions, endogenizing pre-labor-market conditions. We develop a heterogeneous-agent life-cycle model where parents invest in their children’s pre-college human capital at multiple stages to compete for limited college slots. Applying the framework to China—where admissions rely solely on score ranks and enrollment has grown tenfold over the past 25 years—we find that score-based admissions increase the importance of human capital at the college admission stage relative to initial endowments. Family resources therefore shape admission indirectly through parental investment in pre-college human capital. Expanding college access under this system reduces intergenerational mobility because higher-income families respond by disproportionately increasing pre-college investments, strengthening the link between child achievement and parental income. Counterfactuals show that mobility would improve with college expansion if endogenous parental investment responses were shut down.

title: When Meritocracy Fails: College Expansion and the Rise of Intergenerational Persistence

abstract: We investigate how school closures affect educational outcomes through parental responses. Using quasi‐experimental variation in school‐level closure days and linked administrative‐survey data, we find that 10 additional closure days raise private tutoring expenditure by 4.1% and within‐school test‐score dispersion by 25%; over the average 53‐day closure, low‐income students lose 0.09 SD. To quantify substitution between schooling and parental investment and evaluate compensatory policy, we estimate a tournament model in which schooling and tutoring jointly produce test scores. Tutoring substitutes for in‐person days, burdening low‐income households disproportionately. Counterfactuals show a means‐tested voucher fully offsets the resulting rise in inequality.
title: Mitigating School Closures: Parental Responses and Tutoring Vouchers

abstract: In a green transition, workers will have to move from polluting, carbon-intensive sectors to other sectors and firms. To shed light on adjustment costs for workers in the green transition, this column uses German administrative data to estimate the cost of involuntary job displacement for workers in high-carbon-intensity sectors. Such workers face larger earnings and wage losses than workers displaced in other sectors. Production processes in carbon-intensive sectors are also regionally concentrated and involve specific occupations and tasks with higher firm-wage premia, reducing worker options for finding jobs with similar skill requirements and pay.
authors: César Barreto, Robert Grundke, Ze’ev Krill
title: The cost of job loss in carbon-intensive sectors: Evidence from Germany

abstract: Mortality is one of the most salient consequences of climate change. Existing estimates have largely focused on the direct effects of local heat exposure. This column argues that this perspective can miss an important part of the overall health burden. New evidence based on fluctuations in global temperature suggests that climate change also affects mortality indirectly through its effects on economic activity and living standards. Accounting for these broader channels substantially increases estimated mortality damages and highlights an important role for economic resilience in limiting the health consequences of climate change.
authors: Adrien Bilal, Diego Känzig, Krzysztof Lisiecki
title: The mortality costs of climate change

abstract: This paper introduces the notion of $$\mathcal {G}$$ -rules, which extend the Pareto rule when populations are endogenous. Societal evaluations of lives are required. $$\mathcal {G}$$ -rules compare pairs of allocations whenever evaluating the gains of some agents—utility gains or benefits of (not) being born—against the losses of others is not required. $$\mathcal {G}$$ -efficiency naturally arises. The $$\mathcal {A}$$ and $$\mathcal {P}$$ criteria of Golosov et al. (2007) are special cases. Transitive $$\mathcal {G}$$ -rules admit an axiomatic foundation based on normatively appealing properties and can be conveniently represented with $$\mathcal {G}$$ -nondecreasing critical levels. Many public policies that distort fertility decisions are $$\mathcal {G}$$ -efficient because they benefit children who are (not) born as a result of these policies.
title: Generalizing the Pareto principle with endogenous populations

abstract: Asymmetric trading costs arise when shipping times from point i to point j differ from shipping from point j to i. We show that such asymmetric trading costs predict distinct patterns of location in a class of models using Anderson-Dixit-Stiglitz preferences, where advantage in import market access (or potential) is more beneficial than that in export market access. We bring this prediction to the data, as well as additional ones along the lines of a number of propositions, while also controlling for local micro-geographic characteristics and using data on the location and sizes of cities in ancient Greece. Prevailing winds create an environment of asymmetric and seasonally varying trading costs in ancient Greece. We find that trade potential is strongly associated with the location and size of poleis. The model’s directional prediction is supported when trade potential is measured using the left and right eigenvector centralities implied by the model: import-oriented centrality has a larger coefficient than export-oriented centrality. The result is less robust for alternative reduced-form measures. Using 2SLS methods for population-weighted market access, we find significant differences between export and import market access, with the former often more important than the latter. These findings show that directional asymmetries in trading costs matter for urbanization, while also suggesting that their empirical implications depend on how directional access is measured.
title: Asymmetric trading costs and ancient Greek cities

abstract: We study the welfare effects of removing explicit and implicit fossil fuel subsidies, the latter via corrective pricing of local air pollution. We map a multi-region general-equilibrium model with global supply chains to granular data on subsidies, marginal external costs, and national income and product accounts. On average, unilateral subsidy removal raises a country’s welfare by 3.2%, generates revenues equal to 3.1% of consumption, and lowers the carbon price needed for Paris targets by 46%. Non-market gains exceed market losses in most countries. Local air pollution pricing drives 97% of net benefits; removing explicit subsidies alone has minor effects on welfare and emissions. A quarter of countries would already reach their Paris climate target, making additional carbon pricing redundant. Combining subsidy removal with carbon pricing dominates carbon pricing alone everywhere. Global multilateral subsidy removal cuts emissions by 27.4% and raises global welfare, excluding climate benefits, by 2.3%. Corrective fossil fuel taxation can align economic, fiscal, and climate goals. (JEL C68, H23, Q43, Q58)
title: The welfare effects of explicit and implicit subsidies on fossil fuels
